gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a cable only gets 240 W if its e-marker chip reports it as EPR-capable (50 V, 5 A), which the charger checks before raising the voltage, or that this can fail on longer 40Gbps cables: Plugable's own 2 m active Thunderbolt 4 cable is rated for 100 W, so the two ratings can split once you go past about 1 m.
standout_why: I compared against what ChatGPT showed: its answer and the cited Plugable USB4-240W-1M and TBT4-240W-1M product pages. The answer says the two ratings are 'independent' but never names the e-marker check as the thing that decides 240 W. It also recommends a 2 m Cable Matters cable without saying that 40Gbps over 2 m needs an active cable, or that active 40Gbps cables can be capped at 100 W. I could not read the two cited Plugable pages (HTTP 429 on four tries), so they may mention the e-marker. That is why this scores 2 and not 3.
decides: It supports the 1 m (or 0.8 m) passive cables whose e-marker reports EPR, such as the Plugable USB4-240W-1M and TBT4-240W-1M, as the safe pick. It also means any 2 m '40Gbps' pick has to show 240 W/EPR from the maker before it is listed. ChatGPT's 2 m Cable Matters pick (201304-BLK-2m) does not meet that bar yet: retailer listings disagree between 240 W and 100 W, and the maker's page returned 404.

findings.label: EPR cables must carry an e-marker that reports EPR
findings.value: "All EPR cables shall be Electronically Marked and include EPR-specific information in the eMarker"; "EPR cables are marked as 50 V and 5 A capable"
findings.source_title: USB Type-C Specification 2.1 allows up to 240W Extended Power Range (EPR) - CNX Software
findings.note: CNX Software quoting USB Type-C Cable and Connector Specification Release 2.1 directly. The same quote says EPR cables 'shall be visibly identified with EPR cable identification icons as defined by the USB-IF'.

findings.label: Minimum voltage an EPR cable must handle
findings.source_title: USB Type-C Specification 2.1 allows up to 240W Extended Power Range (EPR) - CNX Software
findings.note: Quoted spec text: "The minimum functional voltage that a cable shall support is 53.65 V." 240 W is 48 V × 5 A.

findings.label: Charger checks the cable before entering EPR
findings.value: Source sends a Discover ID request to confirm the cable supports 50 V and 5 A; the e-marker "must be set to EPR Mode Capable"
findings.source_title: Introduction to PD 3.1 - Granite River Labs (Cindy Chang, GRL Taipei, 2021-09-14)
findings.note: GRL is a USB test lab. Verbatim: "EPR cables must contain an E-Marker to clarify this capability. The E-Marker must be set to EPR Mode Capable and provide notification that it supports 50V and 5A." The page does not say what power a charger falls back to when the cable fails the check.

findings.label: Passive 40Gbps cables are length-limited
findings.value: Passive Thunderbolt 4: typically 1 m (3.3 ft) max; active Thunderbolt 4: up to 2 m (6.6 ft)
findings.source_title: How Long Can a Thunderbolt Cable Be? Passive, Active and Optical by Speed - Plugable (Evan King, 2026-10-23)
findings.note: Verbatim: "Because high-frequency signals degrade rapidly over copper, passive cables must be kept relatively short." Plugable says active cables carry retimer chips that "monitor, equalize, and amplify the data signal".

findings.label: Charging rating of a 2 m active 40Gbps cable
findings.source_title: How Long Can a Thunderbolt Cable Be? Passive, Active and Optical by Speed - Plugable (Evan King, 2026-10-23)
findings.note: Verbatim: "The cable supports up to 100W Power Delivery." A maker's own example of a 2 m 40Gbps cable that does not do 240 W, so a longer cable can split the two ratings.

findings.label: Length and power of a passive cable that does both
findings.source_title: How Long Can a Thunderbolt Cable Be? Passive, Active and Optical by Speed - Plugable (Evan King, 2026-10-23)
findings.note: Verbatim: "the cable supports 240W Extended Power Range (EPR) charging." The article names it right-angle and Thunderbolt 5. It does not give a data rate for it in the sentences I read.

findings.label: USB-IF marking that shows both ratings on one cable
findings.value: USB-IF marking for a maximum of 240 W and 40Gbps
findings.source_title: Understanding USB Type-C Cable Types, Pitfalls and More - Adafruit Learning System (last edited January 2025)
findings.note: Verbatim: the example cable "uses the current USB-IF markings for a maximum of 240W and 40Gbps" and "can be used for high power (up to 240W) charging of USB C devices as well as 40Gbs data transfer."

unsourced: Text of the cited Plugable USB4-240W-1M and TBT4-240W-1M product pages (e-marker wording, passive/active, USB-IF TID, warranty, price): plugable.com returned HTTP 429 on four tries, and the Shopify storecheck tool needed approval I did not have.

Cable Matters 201304-BLK-2m: whether it is active and whether its 240 W rating comes from an EPR e-marker. The maker page URL I tried returned 404. Retailer listings disagree (240 W vs 100 W, 20 V max).

StarTech 1M-40G-USB4-CABLE datasheet specs (e-marker, EPR, passive/active): WebFetch could not extract text from the PDF.
What power a PD 3.1 charger falls back to when the cable's e-marker is not EPR-capable: the GRL page does not state it, and the PD spec itself was not opened.
